title: Bhrigu finds food is Brahman
hookLine: a young man asks his father what Brahman is, and the first answer he finds is food
carry: food is brahman: never speak ill of it

cards: A son goes to his father with one request. Teach me Brahman, he says: the ultimate reality, the ground of everything. His name is Bhrigu.
His father is Varuna. And Varuna doesn't lecture. He gives a riddle and sends him away to work it out.
Bhrigu goes off, sits with it, practices, and comes back with an answer that might seem almost too ordinary for the question. He says: food. A run of days on food as practice starts with that answer.

teach.b: The story is in the Taittiriya Upanishad. Varuna's riddle, paraphrased: that from which beings are born, by which, once born, they live, and into which they return, seek to know that. That is Brahman.
And one instruction: seek it through tapas, disciplined, inward effort.
So Bhrigu does, and he comes to see, the text says, that food is Brahman. From food beings are born. By food they live.
Into food they return. It fits every line of the riddle. Now the twist.
Varuna doesn't say, well done, you're finished.
He gives the same instruction again, seek it through tapas, and sends him out once more. Step by step Bhrigu goes deeper: to breath, to mind, to understanding, and at last to bliss. Three things.
First, food isn't thrown away when he goes deeper. It's the first floor of the house, and the house stands on it. Second, the Upanishad draws vows out of it.

teach.h: DO NOT SPEAK ILL OF FOOD
teach.b: Do not speak ill of food. Do not despise food. Make much food.
Not diet rules but a stance: food handled with respect, because it was the first thing Bhrigu found holy. Third, the Ayurvedic texts arrive somewhere close from another direction.

Charaka treats food as what sustains the life of living beings, the ground health is built on, which is why these days give food a whole week. So food as practice doesn't start with a rule about what to eat.
It starts with seeing what food is.

how: In Hindu homes that keep these customs, food is offered before it is eaten, and complaining about food or wasting it is avoided, a stance the Taittiriya Upanishad puts as a vow not to speak ill of food.

o: a fast kept until the mind can see Brahman clearly
food handled with respect, as the first thing Bhrigu found holy
a strict set of rules about which foods are allowed

p: the son who asks, teach me Brahman
the father who answers with a riddle

s: Varuna answers Bhrigu with a full definition of Brahman
he gives a riddle and sends him to seek it through tapas.
after food, Bhrigu goes on to breath, mind, understanding and bliss
his father sends him back each time, and he goes deeper.
the Upanishad's vows include: do not speak ill of food
it also says do not despise food, and make much food.

games.q: you're Varuna. your son comes back from his search and says, food is Brahman. what do you do?
o: send him out to search again, through tapas.
tell him food has nothing to do with Brahman.
games.why: Varuna repeats the instruction to seek through tapas, and Bhrigu goes deeper, to breath, mind, understanding and bliss. Food isn't wrong; it's the first floor.

practice: Bring to mind the last thing you ate, then follow it backward: the hands that served it, the kitchen, the shop, the truck, the field or the sea, the rain and the sun that ripened it.
Go slowly, as far back as you can, and let it become a long line of things you didn't make. If you pray, give thanks for one link in that line.

wordCard.voice: Food as practice. In the Taittiriya Upanishad, food is the first thing Bhrigu recognizes as Brahman, and the vow that follows: do not speak ill of food. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: anna, food. In the Taittiriya Upanishad, Bhrigu first comes to see that food is Brahman.

carryVoice: Your line: food is Brahman, so never speak ill of it. Bhrigu's first answer was food, and he never threw it away. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Taittiriya Upanishad 3.1–3.2 (Bhrigu asks Varuna; the riddle; seek through tapas; food is Brahman)
Taittiriya Upanishad 3.7–3.9 (do not speak ill of food; do not despise food; make much food)
Charaka Samhita, Sutrasthana 27 (food sustains the life of living beings)
